simulatedPerson.name: landscapes
simulatedPerson.hiddenRule: Likes distant exterior shots (85%); dislikes close shots (5%); otherwise 30%.

draftInterpretation: Across 70 stills from 30 films you liked 32 (46%). What follows compares the stills you liked with the ones you did not; it describes your choices in this collection, not a fixed type.

Clearly, distant shots (wide and extreme wide shots: the setting dominates the figures): you liked 23 of 31 (74%), against 23% of the rest, across 16 films. For example: 2001: A Space Odyssey: Frank Poole adrift in space beside the EVA pod; Dr. Strangelove or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb: The B-52 banking over snow-covered mountains; Lawrence of Arabia: The train attack.

Possibly, wide shot (whole figures with substantial surroundings): you liked 17 of 23 (74%), against 32% of the rest, across 15 films. For example: 2001: A Space Odyssey: Frank Poole adrift in space beside the EVA pod; Dr. Strangelove or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb: The B-52 banking over snow-covered mountains; Lawrence of Arabia: The train attack.
You were less drawn to monochrome (12 of 40 liked). That is a description of your judgments, not a gap to correct.

These cannot yet be told apart from the characteristics above, because they occur in nearly the same works: deep focus with distant shots, leading lines with distant shots and no figures with distant shots.
Too few examples to say anything yet about vehicle (2 judged) and extreme close-up (2 judged).

signature.summary: A clear leaning towards distant shots. Early signs of a leaning towards wide shot. Possibly less drawn to monochrome.

terminology.label: dense composition
terminology.definition: The frame is filled with many figures or objects.

terminology.label: leading lines
terminology.definition: Lines in the set or landscape draw the eye towards a point.

terminology.label: off-centre subject
terminology.definition: The main subject is placed clearly to one side.

terminology.label: moderate detail
terminology.definition: A mix of even areas and textured ones.

terminology.label: no figures
terminology.definition: No people are visible.

terminology.label: single figure
terminology.definition: One person.

terminology.label: deep focus
terminology.definition: Near and far planes are both sharp.

terminology.label: shallow focus
terminology.definition: Only one plane is sharp; the rest is soft.

terminology.label: blue
terminology.definition: Blues.

terminology.label: ambient light
terminology.definition: No single directional source; light is even or diffuse.

terminology.label: artificial light
terminology.definition: Electric light from sources outside the frame.

terminology.label: daylight
terminology.definition: Sun or sky light.

terminology.label: moderate colour
terminology.definition: Natural colour intensity.

terminology.label: monochrome
terminology.definition: Black and white, or a toned print (sepia, blue) with a single tint and no colour variety.

terminology.label: muted colour
terminology.definition: Desaturated colour; greys and earth tones dominate.

terminology.label: exterior
terminology.definition: Outdoors.

terminology.label: interior
terminology.definition: Indoors.

terminology.label: close shots
terminology.definition: Any shot from medium close-up to extreme close-up: the frame is mostly face, body or object.

terminology.label: distant shots
terminology.definition: Wide and extreme wide shots: the setting dominates the figures.

terminology.label: medium close-up
terminology.definition: Head and shoulders.

terminology.label: wide shot
terminology.definition: Whole figures with substantial surroundings.

terminology.label: cool
terminology.definition: The image leans towards blue, teal or green.

terminology.label: neutral
terminology.definition: No strong lean towards warm or cool, or an untoned black-and-white image.

limitations: Associations describe this person's judgments of this library only; they are not a comparison with other people.
Characteristics that always appear together in the works judged cannot be separated and are reported together.
Strength labels come from exact tests corrected for the number of characteristics tested; tentative findings may disappear with more judgments.
